The fwdcentaur extension for VS Code

A working guide for build 0.0.2-507.geaa4a48 of the extension and 0.0.1-507.geaa4a48 of the daemon, both built from main at eaa4a48, first written on 2026-09-28 for build 0.0.2-122.gfd90484 and brought up to date on 2026-09-30 from eaa4a48's code: extensions/vscode/src/*.ts, extensions/vscode/package.json, the page in crates/fwd-web and the CLI. Where a design document says otherwise, the guide follows the code and says so. Its screenshots show that build: the ones whose content that build changed were retaken from it on 2026-09-30, and the four it draws as before (a review's steps, an open task's Claim, a highlight's page, and a step's thread in the editor) are kept from the earlier builds.

How to reload it, in short

After installing a new VSIX: press Cmd+Shift+P and run Developer: Reload Window; the page panel comes back by itself on the route it showed, with the same current task (since build 0.0.2-530). A daemon restart needs no reload: the editor joins the daemon again by itself. When the daemon comes back on another build, the page in the panel shows a bar above its header offering this same reload, which loads the page of the newest VSIX installed (section 1.3, when the daemon restarts). Section 1 has the build and install commands, and section 7 says what to reload for each kind of staleness.

The extension exists so that you see in the editor where people and agents are talking about the code, can start such a conversation on the lines you are looking at, and can work through a task's checklist beside the code it points at. It puts four things on screen: the web UI's page in a panel, an inbox in the sidebar, highlights and comment threads on code (in files and on both sides of git diffs), and two status-bar items. It also adds its own items to the editor's right-click menu.

1. Installing and reloading

A build of the extension is a VSIX file stamped with the commit it came from. Installing a new one and reloading the window is how a change to the extension, to the page or to the extension host's node reaches your editor. A daemon restart needs neither: the editor joins the daemon again by itself (section 1.3, when the daemon restarts).

1.1 Building a VSIX

From the repository root. The first two builds are needed only when their crate changed, or once on a fresh checkout:

# the extension host's node: fwd-core compiled to wasm for Node (crates/fwd-host)
(cd crates/fwd-host && wasm-pack build --target nodejs)

# the page (crates/fwd-web), which the VSIX carries its own copy of
scripts/build-web.sh

cd extensions/vscode
npm install        # once
npm run build      # stamps the version, copies the node and the page into dist/, bundles
npm run package    # makes fwdcentaur-0.0.2-<count>.g<hash>.vsix here

npm run build works out the build's version (version.mjs): package.json's 0.0.2, then the number of commits in HEAD's history (git rev-list --count HEAD), .g and the short hash, and .dirty.<UTC time> when the checkout has changes not committed. It writes that to dist/version.json. npm run package does not build: it reads dist/version.json and gives the VSIX the same version and whatever dist/ holds, so run npm run build first every time. The commit count comes before the hash so that VS Code orders builds by it, and a later build installs over an earlier one without --force.

The repository pins its Rust toolchain in rust-toolchain.toml: 1.98.1, with rustfmt, clippy and the wasm32 target (docs/DECISIONS.md, D90: the repository pins its Rust toolchain in rust-toolchain.toml, and CI reads it). rustup installs that toolchain the first time a build in the checkout needs it, and the first build with it compiles everything from scratch, which takes several minutes. cargo install --path crates/fwd, scripts/build-web.sh and wasm-pack all build with it.

The page is copied, not rebuilt.

npm run build builds the page only when crates/fwd-web/dist holds no wasm yet; otherwise it copies what is there. After a change to crates/fwd-web, run scripts/build-web.sh before npm run build, or the VSIX carries the old page.

1.2 Installing it and reloading the window

code --install-extension extensions/vscode/fwdcentaur-0.0.2-<count>.g<hash>.vsix
# without `code` on the PATH:
"/Applications/Visual Studio Code.app/Contents/Resources/app/bin/code" --install-extension …

code --list-extensions --show-versions | grep fwdcentaur
# synestheticsystems.fwdcentaur@0.0.2-507.geaa4a48   (the build this guide describes)

Then, in each open VS Code window, press Cmd+Shift+P and run Developer: Reload Window. The reload restarts the window's extension host, and the extension activates again once VS Code has finished starting: it runs fwd daemon start (which starts the daemon when none runs) and fwd daemon status in the window's first workspace folder, and joins a new node to that folder's project.

After a reload the page panel comes back by itself, on the route it showed and with the task it had current (the extension registers a webview panel serializer, and keeps the current task and the last route in the workspace state); a panel left in a background tab restores its task once shown. Until the panel shows, no task is current (section 3.6, the current task).

Each VS Code window runs its own copy of the extension: its own node, its own panel and its own current task. They all talk to the one daemon your user runs.

1.3 When the daemon restarts

Upgrading the daemon means installing the new binary and replacing the running process, since one daemon serves every project of your user and keeps running whatever binary started it:

cargo install --path crates/fwd
fwd daemon stop
fwd daemon start        # other fwd commands start it too when they need it

Three things then happen to what VS Code shows:

  • The editor follows the project again by itself. When the daemon stops, the extension host's node loses its socket, and the extension asks fwd daemon status after one second, then after two, four and so on up to thirty seconds, until the daemon answers for the window's project. It never starts a daemon itself: one stopped to install a new build stays stopped until something else starts it, such as any fwd command. Once the daemon answers, on its old port or another, the extension joins a new node to it and moves every thread, highlight, whole-file badge and the fwd inbox view onto that node, each keeping what it showed until the new node answers, so that nothing empties while the node changes. Until then Mark read and Dismiss, which write through the node, fail with a message, while everything that runs the fwd binary (a new comment, question or step, Reply, Resolve, Unresolve, Edit, a step opened from the page) still reaches the daemon, starting it when none runs; what it writes shows in the editor once the new node hears it.
  • The page in the panel gets back in by itself, on the route it was on, as long as the daemon comes back on the same port (it tries the port it had last time first). Each time the page's connection drops, the bridge (a small script the extension runs in the panel before the page starts) has the extension register the panel's origin with the daemon again, since a restarted daemon has forgotten it, and the page's own retries then succeed. If the page stays disconnected, run fwd: Show Inbox Page or fwd: Show Task Graph: a page that failed to boot or lost the daemon gets a new document, built for the daemon as fwd daemon start and fwd daemon status find it then.
  • A page that loaded the old build says so. An open page keeps the code it loaded, while the daemon may now run another build. So that you are not left reading what the old build draws, the page notes the build the daemon names when the page boots, asks again each time its connection comes back, and once the two differ shows a bar above its header, whose tooltip names both builds. In a browser tab the bar's Reload page loads the daemon's new page. In the panel the page's files come with the extension, not from the daemon, so the bar says so and offers Reload window, which reloads the window and with it loads the page of the newest VSIX installed; the panel comes back by itself after it. The page never reloads by itself, since a reload loses a reply being written, and the bar goes away if the daemon comes back on the page's own build.

1.4 Which fwd the extension runs

The setting fwd.path names the binary. Empty, the default, means fwd on the extension host's PATH (looked up once, when the extension activates), else ~/.cargo/bin/fwd, where cargo install puts it and which the PATH of a VS Code started from the Dock often lacks. The daemon the extension starts is that same binary re-run as fwd daemon serve, as the setting's description says. Every call passes --format json, and --as <handle> when fwd.as is set.

2. What the extension puts on screen

2.1 The page, in a panel

The panel exists so that the Inbox, Questions, Tasks, Decisions, Graph and Scopes pages a browser shows at fwd ui sit beside your code, and so that a step or a highlight clicked there opens its lines in the editor. It is the same app as the daemon's page (crates/fwd-web), shipped inside the VSIX and run in a webview (a panel VS Code gives an extension for its own HTML) as a node of its own, with its own connection to the daemon.

  • Opening it. fwd: Show Inbox Page opens it on the inbox and fwd: Show Task Graph on the graph, from the command palette; the fwd inbox view's title bar has Show Task Graph too. Opening a notification about a task or a decision in the fwd inbox view opens the page on it, and so do the links in a thread: a task, a decision or a scope a comment names, each task on a highlight's line of what it is joined to and that line's count of messages, and the thread's fwd: Open the Highlight on the Page (section 2.4, comment threads). There is one panel, titled fwd, opened beside the active editor; a command moves an open page to its route instead of opening a second one.
  • Pinned to the window's project. The header shows the project's name and no project selector; after the name, on the Questions, Tasks, Decisions and Graph pages, the one scope selector those four pages share (section 6, the page's pages).
  • Acting as the project's person, not as fwd.as: the as picker in its header switches.
  • A task or a decision fills it, with Back. So that what you read in the narrow panel gets the whole view, and you get back to where you were (VS Code gives a webview no back button), a task you open anywhere on the page (a row of the list, a lozenge, a node of the Graph, a task on an inbox card) fills the panel, and so does a decision you open from a task's panel or from any page but the Decisions page (a lozenge, a decision an inbox card or a question names, the Graph's panel). Its first line has ← Back at its start, which returns to where you opened it from and names that place on hover, and Restore at its end, which, like Esc, gives the list its place back. Back brings that place back as you left it: the Graph at the same scope, zoom, show-closed choice and scroll; the Inbox with the same card selected, which takes the keyboard again, and unread only as it was; the Tasks and Decisions lists with their filters as they were; and a task or a decision whose panel a lozenge opened this one from, full screen again if it was then (section 6, the page's pages). A decision opened from the Decisions list itself opens in the page's own panel beside the list (beneath it under 900 px), as in a browser tab, with no Back.
  • Its text is the workbench's. The page takes its font and size from the variables VS Code gives every webview: the workbench's font at 13 px, and its lines of code in the editor's font and size. A browser tab keeps the page's own 14 px, so the same page reads smaller in the panel.
  • Hidden, it is dropped. Another editor opened in the panel's group hides the page, and VS Code throws its document away; shown again, the page boots again on the route it was on, and a task it was on opens full screen with Back leading to the list. Everything else on it (filters, zoom, the inbox's selection, a reply you had started typing, where Back led) is lost.
  • It keeps its own colours rather than VS Code's theme.

Section 6 walks through its pages.

2.2 The fwd inbox view

The fwd inbox section of the Explorer sidebar exists so that your notifications are in sight without opening the page. It lists the notifications of the principal the extension acts as (fwd.as, else the project's person) that are not dismissed, in fwd inbox's order: unread first, then by priority (now, next, later), then oldest first. Each item reads type: text, for example mentioned: @dnorman the backoff waits on the cap…, with its priority and "unread" beside it, a closed envelope while unread and an open one after; its tooltip is the notification's JSON. What one author did on one task while you had not read it (steps added, comments on the task or on its steps' highlights) is one item, of type digest, reading its latest comment (docs/DECISIONS.md, D95: a burst of comments and additions from one author on one task reaches a person as one notification).

  • Click an item to open what it is about: a notification about a highlight opens the highlight in the editor (section 5, from a step to the code), one about a task or a decision opens the page on it, any other opens the page's inbox. Opening marks it read.
  • Mark read (unread items only) and Reply… sit on the item's row; Reply… asks for the text and runs fwd reply <notification> "<text>", which also marks it read. Dismiss is on the item's right-click menu.
  • The view's title bar has Refresh, which runs the query again (the view follows the project by itself; nothing polls), and Show Task Graph.

2.3 Highlights

A highlight is an anchor with at least one thread whose first message is not resolved: lines that someone is still talking about. The extension draws each one so that you notice those lines while you read. An anchor whose threads are all resolved keeps them, marked resolved, and draws nothing.

Highlights show on every open document of a file inside the window's first workspace folder: the file itself, and the other sides of VS Code's git diffs (the index, HEAD, a commit), each placed where that version has the lines. They move with your edits as you type, the drawn highlight and the hover together, and lines added right above a highlight move it down rather than grow it; after each save, and whenever the document again matches the file on disk (VS Code re-reading a file an agent wrote), the CLI places them again (fwd anchor list --path <file> --against worktree).

2.4 Comment threads and the hover

So that a conversation about lines sits where it happens and covers as little of the code as VS Code allows, each thread is a box VS Code draws under its lines, and fwd decides only what goes in it. Each first message on an anchor is one thread, and its replies are the thread's comments, oldest first, each with its author's handle and its age. Threads start closed (section 3.4, opening a thread, says what opens one).

  • The title bar holds the thread's label on the left and its actions on the right. A thread not resolved has fwd: Resolve (a check mark), and a resolved one fwd: Unresolve; the first thread of a highlight that is a step has fwd: Resolve and Check the Step (two check marks) and fwd: Unresolve and Uncheck the Step instead (section 3.5, replying, resolving, editing). Every thread has fwd: Open the Highlight on the Page, which opens the highlight's own page in the panel, where its lines, everything it is joined to and all its threads show; and while a task is current, Add as a Step of the Current Task (a checklist), which makes the highlight that task's next step (section 3.6, the current task).
  • The label says, joined by ·: on the first thread of a highlight that is a step, Step of “Review: the reconnect loop before it is committed”: not checked, or checked, for each task whose checklist it is on; resolved once the thread is, unless every step it moves with is checked, which says so already; and where the anchor sits when its lines are not there as they were: anchor modified, anchor moved, anchor recovered or anchor partial, and when they are gone anchor orphaned (original lines 6-12), the thread then sitting on the whole file.
  • References are links. A task, a decision, a scope or lines of code a comment names reads as a link that names it in a few words, as its lozenge on the page does: a task by its title cut within 44 characters, a decision by D12 and its title cut within 36, lines of code by where they are, src/retry.rs:6-12 (a whole file by its path alone), as the page and the CLI name them. Its tooltip names it in full, and a click opens a task or a decision on the page, a scope's tasks there, and lines of code in the editor as a step opens them (section 5, from a step to the code). A person reads as @handle, and a message as its first words in brackets.
  • What the highlight is joined to. So that you see which tasks the lines belong to and reach each in one click, the first comment of a highlight's first thread ends with a line of fwd's: step of the tasks it is a step of and code of the tasks whose code it is, each a link that opens the task on the page, then mentioned in how many messages name the highlight (its own threads' not counted), a link to the highlight's own page, which lists them. The line follows the graph as it changes: a step added or taken off, a task linked to the code, a message naming the highlight, a task renamed. A highlight joined to nothing beyond its threads has no line, and the line is fwd's, not the message's: Edit leaves it out.
  • The reply field at every thread's foot is VS Code's one line saying Reply... (section 3.5, replying, resolving, editing). A comment of your own carries Edit, a pencil at the right of its author line, and an edited comment is labelled edited.
  • The hover. Resting the pointer on a highlighted line shows the first three lines of each thread there that is not resolved (300 characters at most), its author, the number of replies, and an open link that opens the thread. The hover works on both sides of a diff.

VS Code also lists the threads of every open file in its own Comments panel, which it opens by itself the first time a file with comments opens; the setting comments.openView set to never stops that.

2.5 The two status-bar items

Left: the current task
Shown while a task is current (section 3.6, the current task): its title, cut at 40 characters, after a checklist icon. Its tooltip says Comments and questions made in the editor go to "<title>". Click to stop. A click clears the current task. Until the node has read the title, it shows the task's first six characters. For five seconds after the editor moves a step, the left of the status bar also says what moved: Step 4 of <title> after Add as a Step of the Current Task, Resolved the thread and checked its step of “<title>” after Resolve and Check the Step, and Set the thread back to active and unchecked its step of “<title>” after Unresolve and Uncheck the Step.
Right: the highlight count
Shown while the active editor's document has a highlight: how many, on lines and on the whole file, after a speech-bubbles icon. Its tooltip reads 2 highlights in this file: comment threads not resolved yet. Click for the next thread. A click runs VS Code's Go to Next Comment Thread.

2.6 The whole-file badge

A highlight on a whole file has no lines to colour, so the file's name carries a ◆ in the Explorer and on its tab, whether the file is open or not, with the tooltip 1 comment thread on the whole file, not resolved yet (fwd). Section 4 has the rest.

3. Highlights and comments

3.1 Commenting on lines, and asking about them

So that what you notice in the code reaches the people and agents working on it, with the lines as its context, a comment or a question starts on the lines you select, and the lines become a highlight whose thread it starts.

  1. Save the file. The CLI anchors the lines of the file on disk, so with unsaved edits the line numbers you select may name other text on disk.
  2. Select the lines. Any part of them will do: the comment takes whole lines, and a selection that ends at the very start of a line leaves that line out.
  3. Right-click and choose fwd: Comment on These Lines. fwd's items sit in a group of their own near the top of the menu, after VS Code's Go to Definition and the others, each titled fwd: …, since VS Code draws no icon in an editor's right-click menu: with a selection, fwd: Comment on These Lines and fwd: Ask About These Lines…; with or without one, fwd: Comment on the Whole File (section 4, whole files); and while a task is current, fwd: Add These Lines as a Step of the Current Task… and fwd: Add the Whole File as a Step of the Current Task… (section 3.6, the current task). The command palette offers the items on lines while text is selected, and those on the whole file while a file's editor is active.
  4. Write the comment in the box that opens, whose placeholder says where it goes: with no task current, For the agents working here: is this related to a task? what should they watch for? @handle mentions a person or an agent: an @ typed at the start, after a space or after an opening mark such as a bracket opens VS Code's completions with the project's people and agents whose name starts with what follows it, each with what it is (person, or the agent's role) and, beside a name two or more of them share, the scopes each one's work is in, and choosing one writes @name, or @ and the start of its id for a shared name, which the bare name would not reach. [[<id>]], with the whole id or its first six characters or more, names a task or anything else, and [[D12]] a decision. Inside backticks nothing is read as a reference.
  5. Send it with one of the box's two buttons, greyed until you have written something. Send to agents runs fwd comment --path <file> --lines 6-12 -- "<text>", which makes the anchor and posts your comment as its first message, for the daemon to pass on (section 3.8, who hears of a comment). Ask runs fwd ask --path <file> --lines 6-12 -- "<text>", which asks no one in particular: the triage agent of the scope your checkout works in hears of it, else the one that serves the whole project, and no one else but whom it mentions (section 3.9, the agents); the answers arrive as replies in the thread. VS Code's draft thread then gives way to the highlight's own thread, drawn over the lines.

If the CLI refuses (an @handle that names nobody, say, or a name two or more principals share, which the refusal lists with each one's id, role and scopes), VS Code shows its sentence as an error and the draft thread stays where it was.

fwd: Ask About These Lines… needs no box: it asks for the question in an input box at the top of the window, whose prompt says it is asked of no one in particular, which the triage agent of its scope answers, and Enter posts it as Ask does. VS Code's own ways to open a comment box, the + in the gutter and Comments: Add Comment on Current Selection (Cmd+K Cmd+Option+C), open the same box with the same buttons, but it says VS Code's Type a new comment: fwd gives a box its wording only while one of its own items opens the box, so that no thread's reply field says it. When the selection's last line ends a thread already there, fwd: Comment on These Lines, like VS Code's command, opens or closes that thread instead of a new box.

3.2 Commenting in a diff: which side

So that you can ask about what a change did where you see it, comments, questions and steps start on every side of a diff that shows the file or a version of it, and each is anchored as that side has the lines.

  • On the file on disk (a file's own editor, and the right-hand side of the working tree's changes, a file under Changes in Source Control), the CLI anchors the lines of the file on disk, as in section 3.1, commenting on lines.
  • On a revision's side (the index on the left of the working tree's changes, HEAD on the left and the index on the right of the staged changes, either side of a commit's diff), every item that anchors lines adds --against the revision (index, HEAD or the commit) and --side of the diff that showed it (base on the left, modified on the right). The CLI then anchors the lines as that revision has them, even when the file on disk no longer does. A click on such a highlight opens the file on disk where the working tree has the lines, as a click on any highlight does (section 5, from a step to the code).
  • A whole file takes a comment or a step on the file on disk only, since a whole file's threads show there and on no revision: a revision's side of a diff has no whole-file items on its menu.
  • Every side shows threads and highlights, each placed where that version has the lines (fwd anchor list --against index, HEAD or the commit). Lines that exist only in the working tree show nothing on the index or HEAD side; a highlight made on a revision shows in the working tree once the CLI finds its lines there; and a side of a diff shows no whole-file highlight (its thread is on the working tree's file). After you stage, the index side is placed again when the git extension serves it again.

3.3 How a comment becomes a thread

In the order it happens:

  1. You press one of the comment box's buttons, or Enter in the input box an item opened.
  2. The extension runs the fwd binary in the workspace folder. The CLI anchors the lines (reading the file on disk and what git holds for it, or on a revision's side of a diff that revision's content), posts the comment through the daemon, and exits.
  3. The daemon stores the anchor and the message; its routing service tells whoever the rules name (section 3.8, who hears of a comment).
  4. The extension host's node hears the new anchor, through its live query on the anchors in that file's path, and then the new message, through a live query on that anchor's messages.
  5. The extension asks the CLI where the anchor sits in each open version of the file (fwd anchor list --path <file> --against <version>) and draws the thread and the highlight there.

So a comment written on the page, from the CLI or by an agent appears in your editor the same way, with no refresh.

3.4 Threads open from the gutter's comment icon

So that clicking or selecting in highlighted code does not unfold its conversation over the code (docs/DECISIONS.md, D98: in VS Code a highlight's thread opens from the gutter's comment icon, not when the cursor enters its lines), a highlight's thread opens and closes when you click VS Code's comment icon in the gutter, on the highlight's last line; the hover's open link opens it too.

  • The cursor or a selection entering or leaving the lines leaves the thread open or closed as it was, and so does a step opened from the page (section 5, from a step to the code).
  • Build 0.0.2-122.gfd90484, which this guide first described, opened the thread a quarter of a second after the cursor or the selection entered its lines, as D47 (the extension shows a highlight's threads inline on focus) had it; D98 narrows that.

3.5 Replying, resolving, editing

  • Reply: the field at the foot of every thread, VS Code's one line saying Reply.... A click opens it to write in, five lines high with Reply beneath, which runs fwd reply <first message> "<text>": a reply is only a reply, never a step. VS Code then empties the field and closes it to its line, and the reply joins the thread when the node hears it. A click elsewhere closes a field with nothing written in it, so it has no Cancel. That first click is VS Code's to ask for: its API gives an extension no way to put the cursor in the field.
  • Resolve (fwd: Resolve, the check mark on the thread's title bar) runs fwd message resolve <first message>. The title bar then says resolved; once every thread on the anchor is resolved, the highlight is no longer drawn and the count drops.
  • Unresolve (fwd: Unresolve, on a resolved thread's title bar) runs fwd message unresolve <first message>, which sets the message back to active. The highlight comes back.
  • On a step's first thread the two read fwd: Resolve and Check the Step and fwd: Unresolve and Uncheck the Step, because there the step moves with the thread (docs/DECISIONS.md, D99: checking a step resolves its highlight's first thread, and resolving that thread checks the step; each control says it does both). Resolving checks the step on every task's checklist the highlight is on, unresolving unchecks it, and the status bar says for five seconds which steps moved. A later thread on the same highlight, and a reply, move alone.
  • Edit, the pencil on one of your own comments (yours are those of the principal the extension acts as: fwd.as, else you), corrects a comment where it stands. It opens the comment in VS Code's editor, holding its text as you would type it again: a person as @handle, a decision as [[D12]], anything else by the first eight characters of its id in double brackets. Save runs fwd message edit <message> -- "<text>": the message keeps its id, its thread and its place, shows labelled edited, and whoever the new text names and the old one did not hears of it. Cancel leaves the text as it was. A refusal (a name that fits nothing, a blank text) shows as an error, and the comment stays in its editor, holding what you wrote, to correct.

Reply, resolve and edit on the page, or fwd reply, fwd message resolve, fwd message unresolve and fwd message edit in a terminal, do the same, and the editor follows. Checking a step on the page or with fwd step check resolves the first thread on its highlight, and unchecking sets it back (section 3.7, a review).

3.6 The current task: comments and questions go to it

While you work through a task on the page (a review, say), what you notice in the code should reach that task, with the code as its context, and a new step should be added only when you ask for one (docs/DECISIONS.md, D92: a new highlight made in the editor with a task current is a comment or a question on that task, with the highlight as its context; adding a step is a separate, explicit action). The current task is how the extension knows which task you are on.

  • How a task becomes current. The page reports each route it goes to, and a route that shows a task makes that task current: #/tasks/<id>, filtered to a scope or not, which is where every task you open in the panel goes, from the list, the Graph, a lozenge or an inbox card (section 2.1, the page in a panel). A route that shows no task (the inbox, the lists, a decision) leaves the current task as it was, so reading the inbox does not end a review. ← Back to a task makes it current again, and Back to a list leaves the current task as it was. The current task is therefore the task the page last showed.
  • What changes. The status bar names the task on the left. fwd's comment box reads A comment or a question on <title>, about this code, and its buttons are Comment on the task and Ask. The right-click menu gains the two step items, the ... menu on a file's editor title bar gains the whole-file one, and every thread's title bar gains Add as a Step of the Current Task.
  • A comment or a question goes to the task. Comment on the task runs fwd comment <task> --path <file> --lines 6-12 -- "<text>": a comment on the task, with the new highlight as its context, which reaches the task's assignee and the triage agent of the task's scope. Ask, and fwd: Ask About These Lines…, run fwd ask --about <task> --path <file> --lines 6-12 -- "<text>": a question asked of no one in particular about the task, which reaches the triage agent of the task's scope and whom it mentions, and not the task's assignee, so that the triage agent answers it first without distracting whoever works the task (docs/DECISIONS.md, D111: a message reaches only whom it is addressed to). Neither makes a step.
  • A step, when you ask for one. fwd: Add These Lines as a Step of the Current Task… asks for the step's first comment in an input box at the top of the window, and Enter runs fwd step add <task> --path <file> --lines 6-12 -- "<text>": the lines become a highlight at the end of the task's checklist, and the comment its first thread, posted once the step exists so that it reaches the task's creator and assignee. fwd: Add the Whole File as a Step of the Current Task… does the same for the file (section 4, whole files). Add as a Step of the Current Task on a thread's title bar makes the highlight the thread is on the task's next step (fwd step add <task> <anchor>), and the status bar says Step 4 of <title> for five seconds.
  • Clearing it. Click the status-bar item, or run fwd: Clear the Current Task. Closing the panel clears it too.
  • Making it current again. The same route reported again changes nothing: the page reports its route each time it boots after being hidden, and a task you cleared stays cleared. Go to another route and back, or close the panel and open the task again.

3.7 A review: a task whose steps are highlights

There is no review type: a review is a task, with "Review" in its title by convention (docs/DECISIONS.md, D40: a review is a task, not a task type). Its checklist is its steps. A step is a step_of edge from anything (a highlight, a message, another task) to the task, and in a review the steps are highlights, because the author is saying "look here" (D41: a step is an edge from any entity to a task, and the highlight is the step). A step is checked when its edge is resolved (D42: the checked state is the step edge's status).

An agent makes one like this:

fwd task create "Review: the reconnect loop before it is committed" --why "…" --done-when "…"
fwd task assign <task> dnorman
fwd step add <task> --path src/retry.rs --lines 6-12 "The loop never backs off: …"
fwd step add <task> --path src/net.rs "Nothing here changes; read it last."   # a whole file
fwd step add <task> <id>       # anything else as a step: a message, a task, a highlight
fwd step list <task>         # [ ] 1. src/retry.rs:6-12 43bda15 `pub fn reconnect(client: &Client) {`, thread open

Working through it, in order:

  1. The assignment reaches your inbox, and what the agent did on the task reaches it as one card while you have not read it: impl-alice added 3 steps and commented 3 times on your task Review: the reconnect loop before it is committed, listing each step with its first comment (docs/DECISIONS.md, D95: a burst of comments and additions from one author on one task reaches a person as one notification).
  2. Open the task on the page, from the card's link or the Tasks page. In the panel it fills the view, with Back; it becomes the current task, and the status bar says so.
  3. The task's Steps section lists the steps in order, with how many are checked. A step that is a highlight reads as fwd step list prints it too: where it is first, src/retry.rs:6-12 (a whole file by its path alone), then the version its lines were chosen in, then its first line as code, so that you find the file before you read the code (Daniel, 2026-09-29: "I think we should reverse the order of code references"). It says whether its first thread is open or resolved, and the task's creator and assignee see remove at the end of each line.
  4. Click a step's line. The editor opens the file at its lines (section 5, from a step to the code), and the cursor lands at their start; the thread stays as it was, and the comment icon in the gutter opens it (section 3.4, opening a thread).
  5. Reply in the thread, and check the step once it is settled: its box on the page, Space on a focused step, fwd step check <task> <n> (the step's number, from 1), or fwd: Resolve and Check the Step on the thread's title bar. Each does both, since checking the step resolves its highlight's first thread and resolving that thread checks the step (D99, the step and that thread move together), and each says so: the box's title reads check the step and resolve its thread. Uncheck the same ways, or with fwd step uncheck.
  6. What you notice along the way becomes a comment or a question on the task, and a new step only when you ask for one (section 3.6, the current task).
  7. A step that no longer belongs on the checklist, because its work moved to other tasks or it was added by mistake, comes off it rather than being checked, which would record it as done. remove at the end of its line, or Delete on a focused step, opens a box for the reason beneath the line; Enter or Remove the step takes it off, as fwd step remove <task> <n> --reason "…" does. For a highlight with an open thread, a choice beneath the box retires it too, resolving its threads so that the editor stops drawing it while its page keeps them, and checking its steps on other checklists; the button then reads Remove and retire (--retire on the command line). Only the task's creator and its assignee see remove, and no one is told.
  8. Finish it with Mark done on the task's panel, or fwd task done <task>. Checking every step does not finish a review; the reviewer does.

The ▸ before a step opens it in place: for a highlight, the lines as they were anchored, its threads with their replies, and a box whose text opens a new thread on the highlight. In the panel, the heading above those lines opens the highlight in the editor.

Key, on a focused stepWhat it does
↑ ↓The step above or below.
Home EndThe first or the last step.
SpaceChecks the step, or unchecks it, and a highlight's first thread with it.
EnterWhat a click on the line does: in the panel, a highlight opens in the editor.
→ ←Opens or closes the step in place.
DeleteOpens the step's removal beneath its line, for the task's creator and its assignee.

The page cannot add or reorder steps yet: fwd step add adds one at the end, and nothing reorders steps. fwd step remove <task> <step> --reason "…" takes one off, as remove does, the step named by its number or by the id of what it is; what the step is stays as it was, a highlight's threads resolved only with --retire.

3.8 Who hears of a comment

The daemon's routing service decides, from what the comment is on and whom it asks. Nobody is told of their own comment, and what one author does on one task while you have not read it (steps added, comments on the task and on its steps' highlights) reaches you as one notification (D95, one notification per author and task). The triage agent, below, is the one that answers first for the scope the comment concerns: the scope of the tasks it is on or near, else the scope your checkout works in, whose own triage agent answers, else the one that serves the whole project (section 3.9, the agents; D122, triage per scope); while neither exists, what would reach it reaches no one through that rule, and a question waits.

What you wroteWho is told
Send to agents, on lines or a whole fileThe triage agent; for each task whose code lies within 50 lines of it in the same file, that task's assignee (a whole file is within reach of every line of it); anyone it mentions.
Comment on the task (a task current)The task's assignee and the triage agent of each of the task's scopes; the assignees of the tasks on code nearby, as for Send to agents; anyone it mentions.
Ask, with a task current or notThe triage agent of the scope the question asks, as a question: the current task's scope (of a task worked in several, the one your checkout works in when it is one of them, else the first), else the scope your checkout works in; with none, or none that has its own triage agent, the one that serves the whole project; and anyone it mentions; no one else, not the task's assignee nor the assignees of the tasks on code nearby, who see it when they open its thread (D111, a message reaches only whom it is addressed to). While no triage agent answers for its scope it waits, listed on every principal's Questions page under a heading for its scope, Asked of the scope Replication, waiting for its triage agent, or Asked of the project, waiting for triage when it asks no scope, and reaches the agent that comes to answer for that scope, as it does.
A step and its first comment, on lines or a whole fileThe task's creator and assignee, whose checklist it is on; the triage agent and the assignees of the tasks on code nearby, as for Send to agents; anyone it mentions.
A replyWhoever wrote the message it answers, whoever started the thread and whoever else wrote in it; for a thread on code, the triage agent and the assignees of the tasks on code nearby, as for Send to agents; for a thread on a task, the task's assignee and the triage agent of the task's scope; anyone it mentions.
An edit of your own commentOnly whoever the new text names and the old one did not.

3.9 The agents: a user of its own for each, and four roles

So that the graph says which agent wrote what, and a question reaches the one agent whose job is to answer it first, every agent working in a project (a Claude Code session, or one of its subagents) has a user of its own there, a principal it names itself, and selects one of four roles for it (docs/DECISIONS.md, D112: each agent has a user of its own, names itself and sets its role; D113: an agent's role is one of lead, triage, implementer or reviewer). You hold no role: you are the project's person, as fwd init recorded you.

lead
A session that coordinates the project's work with you: a project has one per session or worktree doing so, and a Claude Code session one, its own thread, while the agents it dispatches select another role (docs/DECISIONS.md, D119). When it selects the role where no triage agent answers for the scope it works in, fwd prints how and why to start one for that scope as a background subagent.
triage
Answers first for the scopes it serves: a question asked of no one in particular about their work reaches it, and so do comments on their tasks and code, proposals and reviews (section 3.8, who hears of a comment). A scope has one, so its questions have one front line; a small project may instead endorse one to serve it whole, which takes what no scope's own agent takes (D122, triage per scope).
implementer
Works tasks in a scope. As many as the work needs.
reviewer
Reviews what it is asked to review. As many as the work needs.

An agent names itself and selects its role in one command before its first write, fwd principal add <name> --role <role>, and fwd principal role selects another later, while fwd principal rename <name> gives an agent's own principal a new name, keeping its id, work and inbox (refused for a name another principal of the project has); no other command makes an agent's principal, and --as with a name no principal of the project has is refused. A second triage is refused, naming the one that holds the role, and so is a second lead in one Claude Code session, naming the session's lead. fwd principal list lists the project's people and agents, and fwd principal retire takes one that finished its work here off the pickers, while what it did stays attributed to it. The page's pickers of principals (whom a task is assigned to, whom the Ask box asks, whom the page acts as) list them under people, leads, triage, implementers, reviewers and agents (an agent with no role yet). A name is a label that several principals may share (docs/DECISIONS.md, D110): beside a shared name the pickers and the mention search show the scopes each one's work is in, and a command or a mention that gives only the name is refused, listing each one by its id.

How an agent gets its identity. On a machine where fwd's Claude Code plugin is installed, the plugin's hook runs before each Bash command a session runs. It stamps a command made only of fwd (and cd and filters of fwd's output) with the ids Claude Code gives the agent running it, the session's and inside a subagent the subagent's own, and approves it without a permission prompt; fwd then acts as the principal that agent named for itself, since fwd principal add, run stamped, binds the principal to those ids. No --as is needed, and none naming another principal is accepted. An agent relaunched to carry on another's job, a lead after a handoff or the triage agent after a session limit, names itself as the other's successor, fwd principal add <name> --succeeds <old>: the old principal is retired, and its role, its unread notifications and whatever reaches it from then on go to the new one (D114). integrations/claude-code/README.md says how to install the plugin, exactly what the hook stamps and approves, and an agent's first commands. The extension runs fwd unstamped, as you or as fwd.as names (section 2.7, settings).

4. Whole files: the badge and whole-file highlights

Some comments are about a file rather than lines of it ("read this file last"). Such a comment's anchor has no line range (docs/DECISIONS.md, D43: a whole-file reference is an anchor with no line range), so the extension colours no lines for it: its thread sits on the file, and the file's name carries the badge.

  • The badge (◆) shows on the file's name in the Explorer and on its tab while any thread on a whole-file anchor of that file is not resolved, for files that are not open too; its tooltip counts those threads. It comes from a live query on every whole-file anchor in the project.
  • The thread sits on the file rather than on lines, in the working tree only: a side of a diff shows no whole-file highlight.
  • The highlight count in the status bar includes whole-file highlights.
  • An anchor whose lines are gone (anchor orphaned) also puts its thread on the whole file, but it is still an anchor on lines, so it gets no badge.

Making one. fwd: Comment on the Whole File, on the right-click menu with a selection or without and on the ... menu of the editor's title bar, opens fwd's comment box on the whole file, with the buttons of section 3.1, commenting on lines, or of section 3.6, the current task, while a task is current. While a task is current, fwd: Add the Whole File as a Step of the Current Task… asks for the step's first comment and runs fwd step add <task> --path <file> -- "<text>", which makes the whole file the task's next step before it posts the comment, so the task's creator and assignee are told of that comment (section 3.8, who hears of a comment). Both work on the file on disk: in a file's own editor, and on the working tree's side of a diff. When the file already has a thread on the whole file, the comment item opens or closes that thread instead of a new box, as VS Code's own command does: reply there, or comment again from a terminal in the repository:

fwd comment --path src/net.rs "Nothing here changes; read it last."
fwd step add <task> --path src/net.rs "Nothing here changes; read it last."    # instead, to make it a step of the task

5. From a step on the page to the code

A click on a highlight takes you to its code as it is now, always in the same kind of editor: the file on disk, in the normal editor, never a diff, wherever the highlight was made and whatever change its lines lie in (docs/DECISIONS.md, D115: clicking a highlight in VS Code opens the file at its lines in the normal editor, never a diff). In the panel, a click on a step that is a highlight, on a highlight's lozenge, or on the heading of a highlight's lines opens the highlight in the editor, and the page stays where it is. Enter on a focused step does the same. The extension asks fwd anchor show <anchor> where the lines are in the working tree, and opens:

The highlightWhat opensWhere the cursor goes
Made in the file: lines as committed, in a change staged or not, or in a file git does not trackThe fileThe start of the lines
Made on a side of a diff: the index's, HEAD's or a commit'sThe fileThe start of the lines as the working tree has them, not as that side had them
Its lines gone from the working treeThe file, with the message The lines of this highlight are no longer in the working tree; its threads are on the whole file.Nowhere
Its file gone from the working treeNothing, and the message The file of this highlight, <path>, is no longer in the working tree.Nowhere
A highlight on a whole fileThe fileNowhere
  • The cursor goes to the start of the lines, which scroll into view, and the highlight's thread stays as it was: the comment icon in the gutter opens it (section 3.4, opening a thread). A diff you open yourself still shows the highlight on each side that has its lines (section 3.2, commenting in a diff): that is where it shows, not where a click leads.
  • Where it opens. In an editor group other than the page's, the active one when it can; in a new group beside the page when the page is alone.
  • The fwd inbox view opens a notification about a highlight the same way, and so does a link naming lines of code in a thread.
  • A highlight a message names ([[<id>]] in its text) shows beneath the message on the page, as a step shows beneath its task, so that a reply can point at code: its ▸ opens its lines and threads in place, and a click on its line opens it in the editor the same way.

6. The page's pages, and how the page reaches the daemon

The header, on every page: the project's name (in the panel, without a selector); the scope selector (below); the navigation with the count of unread notifications beside Inbox; the as picker (the principal the page acts as, and so whose Inbox and Questions page the navigation opens); the voice picker (for reading the selected card's message aloud with Shift pressed twice, shown only where the browser has an English voice); and the connection's state, Connected once the page has joined the project. Above the header, once the daemon has restarted on another build, a bar offers the reload (section 1.3, when the daemon restarts). Under 640 px, as the panel often is, the header takes three lines, the project and the scope, then the pickers and the connection's state, then the navigation, and lists stack their columns. Everything a page names by a relation shows as a lozenge: rest the pointer on it for a preview, click it to go there. So that a page never says it has nothing while the daemon's answer is on its way, a page says loading… until the daemon has answered, and so does a row, a line or a lozenge's preview naming something the page does not hold, which then says no such task (or decision, message, scope, highlight, principal) when the project has none by that id.

One scope for four pages. So that you follow one scope's work from page to page and choose it once, the Questions, Tasks, Decisions and Graph pages share one scope selector, in the header right after the project's name: all scopes, unassigned (work in no scope), then each scope by its name, active ones first. Each of the four keeps what belongs to the scope chosen, as its part below says. On the Inbox, the Scopes page and a highlight's page, which list nothing by scope, the selector is hidden and its place kept, so that the navigation does not move from page to page. The route carries the choice (?scope=<id>, ?scope=unassigned or ?scope=all), so a reload keeps it, and so do Back, the navigation's links, through a visit to the Inbox or the Scopes page too, and a link that names no scope, such as a lozenge or an inbox card's link. A page freshly loaded has no choice yet, and takes one once the daemon has answered: the scope of the task or the decision its route names (unassigned for a task in no scope), else the scope your own tasks in progress are worked in, else the active scope started most recently, else all scopes.

The Tasks, Decisions and Graph pages show what you open in a panel beside the list (on the Graph, beside the drawing), and beneath it under 900 px. So that a long thread is not read in a narrow column, the panel's Full screen, in its corner at every width, lets it fill the page with the list hidden, until Restore or Esc gives the list its place back; wider than 900 px, dragging the panel's left edge sets its width, which the browser remembers for each page. In the VS Code panel a task you open on the page fills it by itself, with ← Back, and so does a decision you open from a task's panel or from another page (section 2.1, the page in a panel).

The screenshots below are of the page served by a scratch daemon of its own and taken in headless Chromium, as the panel opens it (?lock=1: no project selector, and a task opening full screen with Back) and draws it on a Mac: the four variables VS Code gives a webview for its fonts are set as VS Code sets them there (the workbench's 13 px system font, the editor's 12 px Menlo). The panel runs the same build from the extension's own copy.

Inbox

For answering what people and agents ask of you, and writing down new questions, without leaving the keyboard. At the top, the Ask box records a question that belongs to no task: choose whom it asks, by default no one in particular, of the scope the header's scope filter chooses, the scope Replication, which its triage agent answers (or the project, which the triage agent that serves it whole answers, offered beside it and the default when the filter chooses all scopes), else one of the project's people and agents, and its priority, and Enter sends it. While no triage agent answers for what it asks, the box says that the question waits on the Questions page until one does. Below the heading, the notifications of the principal the page acts as, you unless the as picker says otherwise, as cards, one per conversation, task or decision they point into, newest first, unread only unless you untick it; Mark all read sits beside the heading. Each card says in a line per notification why it is in the inbox, holds the conversation with reply and resolve, and has Mark read and Dismiss. What one author did on one task while you had not read it is one line on the task's card, listing each step and each comment beneath it (D95, one notification per author and task). ↑ and ↓ move between cards; in a reply box Enter sends, Shift+Enter starts a new line and Esc leaves. In the VS Code panel, Back from a task or a decision opened from a card brings the Inbox back with that card selected and unread only as it was.

The for selector beside the heading shows one other principal's inbox instead, so that you can check on an agent without acting as it (docs/DECISIONS.md, D104: the Questions and Inbox pages open on the viewer's own, and show one other principal's at a time only to look). The route keeps the choice (#/inbox?for=<handle>), and a line beneath the heading says whose inbox you are reading. Nothing there changes theirs: Mark all read, Mark read and Dismiss are greyed, the cards have no reply box, and a reply or a move made from a card's rows is yours.

Mentions. In the Ask box, and in every box on the page that writes a message (a panel's comment box, a reply box, the box that edits a message), an @ typed at the start, after a space or after an opening mark, and never in code, opens the mention search: a list beneath the box offers the project's people and agents whose name starts with what you type, eight at most, each with what it is (person, the agent's role, or agent) and, beside a name two or more of them share, the scopes each one's work is in. A click, or ↑ ↓ and then Enter or Tab, writes the mention in place of what you typed; Esc closes the list for that mention. A shared name is written as @ and the first eight characters of the id, since the name alone would be refused.

Questions

For answering what you are asked, the most urgent first. The page lists the questions asked of the principal it acts as: each message that asks them something (fwd ask, a forward), under the priority it wants its answer at, now, then next, then later, each heading saying how many it holds, newest first beneath it; the open ones unless you untick open only. A question asked of no one in particular is the triage agent's that answers first for the scope it asks, listed on that agent's page; while no triage agent answers for it, every principal's page lists it, under a heading for its scope, Asked of the scope Replication, waiting for its triage agent, or Asked of the project, waiting for triage when it asks no scope, above the priorities. Each question is a card with its answers beneath, worked from the keyboard as the Inbox's cards are, and the same Ask box heads the page. The for selector shows the questions asked of one other principal instead, to read without acting as them (D104, one other principal's at a time only to look; the route keeps it as #/questions?for=<handle>): their cards have no reply box.

The header's scope keeps the questions about that scope's work: those about the scope itself, about a task worked in it or about a decision attached to it. Unassigned keeps those about none of these (about nothing, about a highlight alone, about a task in no scope or a ruling for the whole project), and all scopes every question. So that no question asked of you is out of sight without a word, a line beneath the heading says how many more the scope leaves out, with Show all scopes. A question a route names (a lozenge naming a question leads to #/questions/<id>) shows whatever the scope.

Tasks

For finding a task and acting on it. The list holds the tasks worked in the header's scope (unassigned: those worked in no scope), and has a title filter, a label filter and the toggles mine (assigned to the acting principal), ready only and show closed, which in the VS Code panel Back brings back as they were; each row shows the title with its labels and how many steps are checked ("1/3"), the status, readiness, priority, scope, assignee, how many messages it has and when it last changed. New task puts a form in the panel for writing a task with every field fwd task create takes, as the principal the page acts as; Create task, or Ctrl+Enter in any field, makes it.

A task's panel shows its short id (a click copies the whole id), its status, who made it, where it is worked and who is assigned (with a picker of the project's people and agents, grouped by role, that assigns it), its labels (a box adds one and suggests bug and feature first, and a label's button takes it off: docs/DECISIONS.md, D97: a task's kind, such as bug or feature, is a label, not a task type), the moves its status allows you, its readiness, what, why and done-when, its Steps (section 3.7, a review), its relations as lozenges, and its thread with a box for commenting on the task. On the review of section 3.7, in progress and yours, the moves are Submit for review, Mark done, Cancel and Rejustify. A task that is open offers Claim rather than Start: it starts the task and makes you its assignee, in the scope its button names before you click it. That is the scope the task is worked in, whatever scopes you work in, since a start never moves a task out of its scope (docs/DECISIONS.md, D87: starting a task worked in another scope is refused, with a prompt to switch to that scope first); only a task worked in no scope takes a scope, any active one whoever made it, from a picker when there are several. A closed task shows the note it was closed with under Closed because, each whole id or @handle in it drawn as a lozenge. A task shown in the VS Code panel is the window's current task (section 3.6, the current task).

Decisions

For finding a ruling and what rests on it. Every decision by number, one line each with its short id, status, area, the scope it governs or project-wide, and who ruled on it or proposed it, filtered by status and area and by the header's scope. Under a scope the list keeps the rulings that govern the whole project with that scope's own, since the project's rulings apply to every scope's work, so that the list stays short enough to read (docs/DECISIONS.md, D93: a decision may be attached to the scope it governs; one attached to none governs the whole project, and its area is its type); unassigned keeps the project's rulings alone, and all scopes every ruling. A caption by the filters says which rulings the list holds, and a page freshly loaded on a decision opens on the scope that decision is attached to, so that its line is listed. In the VS Code panel, Back to the list brings its status and area filters back as they were. A decision opened from the list shows in the panel its record (context, ruling, consequences), the scope it governs with a picker that attaches it to another or to none, what cites it and what it cites, the moves its status allows as buttons (Accept and Reject on a proposal; Supersede and Repeal on a ruling in force), and its comments. Each move asks for the reason it keeps as a comment on the decision, and Supersede for the ruling that replaces it too; a closed ruling says why it closed in the words of that comment.

Graph

For seeing what waits on what. One scope's tasks at a time, each to the right of what it waits for, joined by "unblocks" arrows; subtasks dotted, proposals as ghosts, a task outside the scope that a dependency joins shown as a muted stub, and on each task the number of its messages. The drawing is of the header's scope (all scopes, unassigned, or one scope); the controls choose the order of each column (auto, which crosses edges as little as it can; priority; status), closed tasks, and the zoom. In the VS Code panel a click on a task opens it on the Tasks page, filling the page, over the list of the tasks of the scope the Graph shows, and so makes it the window's current task; its ← Back brings the Graph back at the same scope, zoom, show-closed choice and scroll. In a browser tab the task opens in the Graph's own panel beside the drawing, which has the Tasks page's Full screen, hiding the drawing, and its edge.

Scopes

For seeing the areas of work the project has, and for making or changing one. One line per scope, with its short id, status and branches, its intention on hover, active scopes first; a scope's name leads to the Tasks page filtered to the tasks worked in it. New scope above the list, and Edit on a line, open a scope's panel beside the list (beneath it in the narrow panel), with its name, intention, repository, branches and status as fields to change in place. Save writes only the fields you changed, under the rules the CLI runs, and shows a refusal (a blank name, branches without their repository) beneath the fields; Revert forgets what you typed, and Close puts the panel away. A new scope is made by the principal the page acts as; a scope has no owner, and anyone works in any scope.

A highlight's page

For reading a highlight where there is no editor, on a phone or in a browser (docs/DECISIONS.md, D47: a highlight's page in the browser shows only the highlighted text), and for seeing everything the highlight is joined to. It shows where it is, src/retry.rs:6-12, as its heading, its basis, who highlighted it, the lines as they were anchored, what it is joined to under References (the tasks it is a step of, the messages that name it, the tasks whose code it is), its threads, and a box that opens a new one. In a browser tab a highlight's lozenge, or a step that is a highlight, leads here. In the panel those clicks open the editor instead (section 5, from a step to the code), and a highlight's thread in the editor leads here: its title bar's fwd: Open the Highlight on the Page, and the count of messages on its line of what the highlight is joined to (section 2.4, comment threads).

How the page and the editor reach the daemon

In the order it happens:

  1. When VS Code has finished starting, the extension runs fwd daemon start and fwd daemon status in the window's first workspace folder. The status names the daemon's port and the folder's project; a folder that belongs to no project gets no node, and the extension says nothing until a command needs one.
  2. The extension loads its node (fwd-core compiled to wasm for Node, keeping everything in memory) and joins it to the project's socket. Its live queries on anchors, their messages, their steps and what points at them, the titles of the tasks a thread names, and notifications feed the threads, the highlights, the badges and the inbox view. When its socket closes, it joins the daemon again once the daemon answers (section 1.3, when the daemon restarts).
  3. A command opens the panel. The extension writes the panel's document: the page's script, wasm and stylesheet from its own dist/web, a Content Security Policy that lets the page load only those files and connect only to them and to the daemon, and the bridge, which runs first.
  4. The bridge puts the daemon's address, the project and lock=1 in the page's URL, and sends the panel's origin to the extension. The daemon refuses any webview's origin it has not been told of, since any extension's webview can run script, so the extension registers this one (POST /webview-origins) and answers the bridge. The page boots then, or after five seconds without an answer.
  5. The page asks the daemon for /health, which names the daemon's build, and /projects, opens the project's socket, and from then on reads with live queries and writes through the same operations the CLI uses. Each time its connection comes back after a drop, it asks /health again, and when the build changed it shows the bar that offers a reload (section 1.3, when the daemon restarts).
  6. From then on the bridge carries only coordination: each route the page goes to (the current task follows it), a highlight the page asks to have shown in the editor, the page's connection state, a new registration of its origin whenever the connection drops, and the bar's request to reload the window.

The rest goes through the fwd binary, one child process per command: starting the daemon, everything that needs git (a new comment, question or step, which anchors lines; where an anchor sits in a version of its file), replies, Resolve and Unresolve, Edit, and a step added from a thread's title bar.

7. When something looks stale

Most staleness comes from a part that loaded something once and keeps it: the extension host's node its connection, an open page its code, a VSIX the page it was built with, the daemon its binary. Each row says which part, and how to make it load again.

What you seeWhyWhat to do
Threads, highlights, badges, the highlight count or the fwd inbox view stop changing; a comment you just sent does not become a threadThe daemon stopped or restarted. The extension host's node joins it again by itself once fwd daemon status answers, which it asks at most thirty seconds apart, but it never starts a daemon (section 1.3, when the daemon restarts)Wait half a minute. If the daemon was stopped, start it: fwd daemon start, or any fwd command. If they still do not follow, Developer: Reload Window; the page panel comes back by itself
The panel's header shows a connection state other than ConnectedThe daemon stopped or restarted; the page registers again and retries by itself when the daemon is back on the same portWait a few seconds. If it stays, run fwd: Show Inbox Page or fwd: Show Task Graph, which gives a page that failed or lost the daemon a new document, starting the daemon if none runs
A row, a lozenge or its preview says loading…, or a page says it and nothing elseThe page has not heard from the daemon since it loaded; once it has, it names what it holds, or says no such task (decision, message…) when the project has none by that idWait a few seconds. If it stays, see the row above
The Questions, Tasks, Decisions or Graph page lacks a question, a task, a ruling or a node you expectedThe header's scope selector keeps only that scope's work, and the choice follows you from page to page and through Back (section 6, the page's pages)Choose all scopes in the selector; on the Questions page, Show all scopes beneath the heading
A bar above the page's header says the daemon restarted on a newer build of fwdThe page keeps the code it loaded, and when its connection came back it found the daemon running another buildIn a browser tab, the bar's Reload page. In the panel, install that build's VSIX if you have not, then the bar's Reload window; the panel comes back by itself
The panel's page lacks a change made to crates/fwd-webThe panel runs the copy of the page its VSIX carries, which npm run build copies without rebuildingscripts/build-web.sh, npm run build, npm run package, install the VSIX, Developer: Reload Window; the panel comes back by itself
A browser tab's page lacks a change made to crates/fwd-webThe daemon serves the page built into its binaryscripts/build-web.sh, cargo install --path crates/fwd, fwd daemon stop, fwd daemon start, reload the tab
code --list-extensions --show-versions names an older build than you packagedThe VSIX was not installed, or was packaged without npm run build first, so it took the last build's version and filesnpm run build, npm run package, install, reload
A highlight in the working tree sits on the wrong linesWith unsaved edits, the extension's own line tracking stands; the CLI places highlights again only after a save, or when the document again matches the file on diskSave the file
A side of a diff places a highlight where that version had it before your last stage or commitA revision is placed when its document opens, and again when the git extension serves it again (the index after a stage)Close the diff and open it again
No threads, highlights or inbox at all, and the page's commands say This window's folder belongs to no fwd project, or fwd could not start its daemon here.The window's first folder resolves to no project, or the extension could not run fwdfwd init in the repository, or set fwd.path; then reload the window
The status bar names the current task by six characters of its idThe node has not read its title yet, or is not connectedWait; if it stays, see the first row
A task you did not mean is currentThe current task follows every task the page shows: one opened from the list, the Graph, a lozenge or an inbox card, and one that Back returns toClick the status-bar item to clear it

8. Reference: commands, keys, settings, CLI

Commands the extension contributes

The extension contributes no keybindings. "Palette" means the command palette (Cmd+Shift+P), which lists only the commands that make sense there: the three page commands, the items on lines while text is selected, those on a whole file while a file's editor is active, and fwd: Clear the Current Task while a task is current. Every command that acts on a thread, a comment or an inbox item is hidden from it (package.json's commandPalette menu), since run from there it would have nothing to act on.

The CLI invocations this guide uses

Each is checked against target/debug/fwd <command> --help at eaa4a48. The extension adds --format json, and --as <handle> when fwd.as is set, and puts -- before comment text.

InvocationWhat it does
fwd daemon startStarts the daemon, or restarts it when it listens the other way than asked; the extension runs it at activation
fwd daemon statusThe daemon's port and projects, and project for this directory; exits 7 when no daemon answers
fwd daemon stopStops the daemon
fwd uiOpens the page in a browser, on this directory's project
fwd comment --path <file> --lines a-b "<text>"Anchors the lines (1-based, inclusive) and posts the first comment: what Send to agents runs
fwd comment --path <file> "<text>"The same on the whole file
fwd comment <task> --path <file> --lines a-b "<text>"A comment on the task, with the new highlight as its context: what Comment on the task runs
fwd comment <id> "<text>"Comments on a task, an anchor, a scope or a decision
fwd ask [--about <task>] --path <file> --lines a-b "<text>"Asks the project about the lines, which become a highlight whose thread the question starts; its triage agent hears of it. What Ask runs
fwd ask --to <handle> "<text>"Asks one person or agent instead of the project
… --against index|HEAD|<commit> --side base|modifiedAdded to any of these that anchors lines: the lines are anchored as that revision has them, which is what the editor adds on a revision's side of a diff
fwd reply <message or notification> "<text>"Replies in the message's thread
fwd message resolve <message>Resolves a message: on a thread's first message, the thread; on a step's first thread, the step is checked too
fwd message unresolve <message>Sets a resolved message back to active; on a step's first thread, the step is unchecked too
fwd message edit <message> "<text>"Replaces the text of a message you wrote, keeping its id and its place
fwd step add <task> --path <file> --lines a-b "<text>"Adds the lines as a highlight at the end of the task's checklist, with the text as its first comment; without --lines, the whole file
fwd step add <task> <id>Adds anything (a highlight, a message, a task) as the next step
fwd step list <task>The checklist in order, with what is checked
fwd step check <task> <step>, fwd step uncheck <task> <step>Checks or unchecks a step, named by its number (from 1) or by the id of its relation or of what it is; a highlight's first thread moves with it
fwd step remove <task> <step> --reason "<why>" [--retire]Takes a step off the checklist; with --retire, resolves a highlight's threads too
fwd anchor show <anchor> [--against worktree|index|HEAD|<commit>]Where the anchor is in that version, the working tree by default: what the extension asks before it opens a highlight
fwd anchor list --path <file> [--against …]Every anchor in the file, placed in that version
fwd task create "<title>" --why "…" --done-when "…"Makes a task
fwd task assign <task> <handle>Makes someone the assignee; they are told
fwd task start <task> --scope <scope>Starts the task in that scope and makes you its assignee; a task worked only in other scopes is refused, naming them. Start runs it with one of the task's scopes, or for a task in none with the scope its button names
fwd task show <task>The task's fields and its checklist
fwd task done <task>Finishes the task
fwd inboxYour notifications
fwd principal list [--all]The project's people and agents, each with what it is (person, lead, triage, implementer, reviewer, or agent for one with no role); with --all, the others too, retired or not belonging here, each saying which
fwd principal add <name> --role lead|triage|implementer|reviewerAn agent names itself and selects its role; run from a Claude Code session with the fwd plugin, it binds the principal to the agent running it
fwd principal add <name> --succeeds <old>An agent relaunched to carry on another's job names itself as its successor: the old principal is retired, and its role, unread notifications and routing move to the new one
fwd principal succeed <old>The same succession, for an agent that is a principal already
fwd principal role <name> <role>Selects another role; a second triage is refused, naming the one that holds it, and so is a second lead in one Claude Code session
fwd principal retire <name>Takes a principal that finished its work off the pickers; what it did stays attributed to it
fwd --as <name> principal bind <name>From a Claude Code session with the plugin, takes over once a principal from before the plugin that no agent is bound to
cargo install --path crates/fwdInstalls the CLI and daemon binary into ~/.cargo/bin
scripts/build-web.shBuilds the page into crates/fwd-web/dist
wasm-pack build --target nodejs (in crates/fwd-host)Builds the extension host's node
npm run build, npm run package (in extensions/vscode)Builds the extension, then makes the VSIX
code --install-extension <vsix>, code --list-extensions --show-versionsInstalls a VSIX; lists what is installed

9. Not built yet, and where the design documents differ

Not built yet

  • Adding or reordering steps on the page; reordering steps anywhere (fwd step add adds one at the end).
  • The panel's page following fwd.as and VS Code's theme colours (it takes the workbench's fonts), and keeping its filters, its drafts and where Back leads while hidden.
  • A remote window (SSH, a container, WSL): nothing forwards the daemon's port to where the panel runs.
  • Threads on the pull-request extension's documents; and on a thread, Link to task, Convert to task, Ask scope and Ask, a label saying whom its first comment reached and whether they have read it, and Reposition for an orphaned anchor (docs/design/vscode-extension.md, Editor comments and highlights).

Where the design documents differ from the code

  • docs/design/vscode-extension.md's list of surfaces still describes a graph panel drawn in React and a scope tree view in the sidebar. What exists is the web UI's page in a panel and the fwd inbox view.
